line: e4 d5 exd5 Nf6 Bb5+ Bd7 Be2
teaches: A check is worth playing when the only ways to answer it all cost the defender something, even if you intend to retreat straight afterwards — forcing a piece onto a square where it blocks its own side's plans buys a concession quiet development never would.
explains: The bishop checked and has now stepped back, having achieved one thing: a black piece stands on d7, wedged between the queen and the pawn on d5. So the queen can no longer take that pawn back — only the knight can. White has spent two moves with the same bishop and still comes out ahead, because the interposition is permanent and the retreat costs nothing.
structural: the interposition is permanent — its checkable claim belongs to Bd7, not to the retreat it is anchored on
